name: Wolff's law facial loading

card.summary: The idea that mechanical load remodels facial bone, borrowed from a real principle of bone biology but untested for tongue posture, chewing or pulling.
card.note: The principle is well supported for bone generally; its application to adult facial reshaping via DIY loading has no published tests.

quick.overview:
Wolff's law is a nineteenth-century principle that bone adapts its structure to the loads placed on it. In looksmaxxing it is the theoretical backbone for mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and bonesmashing: if bone responds to load, the argument goes, loading the face should reshape it.

The general principle, now usually called bone functional adaptation, is well supported by research on bones such as the limbs and spine. Whether the small, specific forces used in facial practices change the adult face has not been tested.
quick.mechanism: Bone cells, especially osteocytes, sense mechanical strain and signal bone-forming and bone-resorbing cells. Frost's mechanostat model proposes thresholds of strain at which bone is added, conserved or lost. The faces' bones are described in orthodontic literature as load-bearing, but the loads in daily tongue posture are small and their effect has not been measured.
quick.risks: The principle itself carries no risk. Practices justified by it, such as forceful pulling or striking of the face, are discussed separately and are not covered by research support.

lead: Wolff's law states that bone in a healthy animal adapts to the loads placed on it, becoming denser and stronger under greater loading and weaker under less [1][2]. It is named for the German surgeon and anatomist Julius Wolff (1836-1902), whose 1892 book Das Gesetz der Transformation der Knochen set out the idea [2][3]. In looksmaxxing communities, 'Wolff's law' is cited as the reason that mewing, chewing, thumb pulling and similar practices are said to reshape the face.

Scientists now generally prefer the term bone functional adaptation: reviewers note that Wolff's original mathematical formulation has been discredited while the broader concept of adaptation to loading is supported by much experimental and observational data [4]. No published study has tested whether tongue posture or other do-it-yourself facial loading remodels the facial skeleton.

paras: When loading on a bone increases, the bone remodels over time to resist it; when loading decreases, it loses density. Reduced loading, for example in astronauts under microgravity, leads to bone loss [2][6]. Only cyclic loading is described as inducing bone formation [2].

Wolff's concept built on earlier work, and Harold Frost later refined it as the mechanostat and the Utah paradigm, which propose strain thresholds. In one formulation, strains below about 50 microstrain accompany the largest disuse effects, while strains above about 1500 microstrain tend to turn on bone modeling that adds and reshapes bone [7][8]. A reviewer for clinicians argues that remodeling alone can remove or conserve bone but not add it, with modeling responsible for adding bone [7].

Remodeling works through mechanotransduction, in which cells convert mechanical signals into biochemical ones. Osteocytes, the most abundant bone cells, are particularly sensitive to fluid flow caused by loading and signal other cells [2][6]. Mechanically sensitive proteins such as PIEZO1 regulate bone homeostasis through osteoblast and osteoclast signalling in mouse research [9].
No studies found testing Wolff's law or bone loading as applied to do-it-yourself facial reshaping through tongue posture, chewing, pulling or striking.

Studies of bone adaptation in general include reviews written for orthodontic clinicians, which list the mandible and maxilla among load-bearing bones [8], and anthropological reviews supporting bone functional adaptation [4]. A clinical study correlated wrist loads with distal radius tilt in 30 wrists [10]. These do not address facial change from home practices.

Proponents of mewing and related practices argue that facial bones are shaped by forces applied over time. One forum guide lists as premises that facial structure is moulded by forces, that facial sutures never fuse, and that forward growth of the maxilla is the goal [11]. Critics in the same discussions and orthodontic bodies say these claims have not been demonstrated; the American Association of Orthodontists states there is no evidence mewing reshapes the jaw [12].

lore.intro: 'Wolff's law' is invoked in looksmaxxing forums as scientific backing for mewing, chewing, pulling and bonesmashing, often with the argument that facial sutures never fuse [11].

claims.claim: Facial bones remodel under mechanical load, so loading the face can reshape it
claims.believers: A forum guide says facial structure is moulded by forces applied over time and that tongue posture can drive forward maxillary growth [11].
claims.experts: Reviews support bone functional adaptation in general and note that jaw bones are load-bearing [4][8]; no study has tested home facial loading in people.

claims.claim: Facial sutures never fuse, so adults can still grow the face
claims.believers: The same guide lists this among its starting premises [11].
claims.experts: Orthodontic sources describe the midpalatal suture as open in children and generally fusing after puberty, so adult expansion needs surgery or implants [13].

claims.claim: Greater force means more bone change
claims.believers: Hard mewing and similar practices are justified by the idea that more pressure produces more remodeling [11].
claims.experts: Mechanostat theory proposes strain thresholds and says that excess strain can also cause microdamage [7]; no study measures the strain produced by facial practices.
